title: 2026 AI in Science Repository
text:
Preface
Science has always been a social and collective endeavor. From the Manhattan Project to the Human Genome Project to the modern AI race, many of the most consequential advances in human knowledge have come not from lone investigators but from coordinated groups working toward shared problems. In the Fall 2026, 2 faculty, 1 postdoc, and 14 PhD students leveraged these principles to collectively make sense of one of the most pressing issues in contemporary research:

How is AI changing the social nature of scientific inquiry, for better and for worse?







Figure 1: Structure of seminar on collective [artificial] intelligence in science.



The seminar began with an introduction to big-team science – its evolution, competitive advantages, and relevance to the current moment1–3. From there, the course became a collective investigation, wherein we worked together to understand the newly disrupted nature of each stage of our research pipelines. This includes project management, literature review, idea development, data collection, analysis, writing, and dissemination4. In an attempt to develop a balanced perspective, we alternated between deploying receptive vs. critical lens, identifying key resources, consensus statements, and areas of disagreement along the way. Ultimately, the goal was to organize our insights into the resource you are viewing right now: the 2026 AI-in-Science Repository.
Each week followed a consistent structure (Figure 1). One component of our research pipeline would be selected for examination (e.g., data analysis). Members of the course would search for key resources for understanding the emerging role of AI. In class, we would then engage in peer-to-peer teaching – all with the goal of identify the top 3 resources to include in the final repository. Last, we used a live online voting platform to solicit, debate, and vote upon key takeaways for the week (https://pol.is/). The result is the the 2026 AI-in-Science Repository: a summary of our top resources, takeaways, and disagreements.




1. Coles, N. A., Hamlin, J. K., Sullivan, L. L., Parker, T. H. & Altschul, D. Build up big-team science. Nature 601, 505–507 (2022).


2. Coles, N. A., Goes Braga Takayanagi, J. F., Grant, G. L. & Basnight-Brown, D. M. The rise, impact, and imbalances of big-team psychology. Psychological Science 37, 287–297 (2026).


3. Coles, N. A. et al. Team scientists should normalize disagreement. Science 384, 1076–1077 (2024).

title: Personal AI Philosophy Statements
text:
The prompt
The collective guide in the preceding chapters records where the seminar converged. This part records where its members did not.
Alongside the shared repository, each participant wrote a personal AI philosophy statement: a short, signed account of how they intend to use — and refuse to use — AI in their own research. The statements were written independently, after the final week, and were deliberately not harmonized. Read together, they are a snapshot of how a single room of scientists, working from the same set of resources, arrived at meaningfully different positions.
Participants were asked to address four questions in roughly 500-1000 words:

title: Personal AI Philosophy Statements
text:
Where do you delegate? At which stages of your research pipeline do you currently use AI, and what do you gain by doing so?
Where do you refuse? What will you not delegate, and on what grounds — epistemic, ethical, professional, or personal?
What would change your mind? Name the evidence or capability that would move one of your refusals into your delegations.
What do you owe others? How will you disclose your use of AI to collaborators, reviewers, readers, and students?

title: Personal AI Philosophy Statements
text:
Reading these statements
Each statement speaks only for its author. Disagreement between statements is the point, not an error to be corrected.
